paras: Rainy days are the best days. Everyone else groans when the clouds roll in, but I cheer. Rain means puddles to stomp in and the sound of drops on the roof at night.

Last Saturday, it rained all morning. My dad looked out the window and sighed. "I wanted to mow the lawn today, Lucia," he said. "Rain spoils everything, and I like sunny days best." I grabbed my yellow boots. "Rain doesn't spoil anything, Dad," I said. "It makes everything better!"

We went outside anyway. I found three worms on the sidewalk and moved them back to the grass. Dad held the umbrella and shook his head, but he smiled a little. I still think rain is the best weather of all.

paras: Rory wanted to ride his bike, but the chain fell off in Grandma Fran's driveway. Grandma Fran knelt down, got her hands greasy, and fixed it in two minutes. Rory buckled his helmet and rode away down the street.
Halfway down the block, Rory stopped. He had forgotten something. He rode back and said, "Thank you for fixing my bike, Grandma." Later he drew her a picture of a bike that said THANK YOU.

stories.title: The High Shelf
paras: Rory wanted his kite from the high shelf in Grandma Fran's closet, so he could fly it at the park. He pulled over a rolling chair and stood on it. The chair wobbled, and Rory grabbed the door just in time.

His grandma hurried in. "That chair could roll away!" she said. She brought the step stool from the kitchen and held it steady while Rory climbed up and got the kite. "Being careful keeps you safe," said Grandma Fran.

texts.title: A Busy Home
paras: Honeybees live together in a home called a hive. A hive can hold thousands of bees, and each bee has a job. The queen bee lays the eggs. Worker bees clean the hive, care for the young bees, and guard the door.

Inside the hive, worker bees build rows of six-sided rooms called cells. They make the cells out of wax from their own bodies. Some cells hold eggs. Others hold honey, which the bees make from nectar they get from flowers. The bees save the honey to eat in winter.

texts.title: From Flower to Flower
paras: Honeybees fly from flower to flower to drink nectar, a sweet juice inside flowers. Back at the hive where they live, they make the nectar into honey. They save some of the honey to eat in winter.

While a bee drinks nectar, a powdery dust called pollen sticks to its fuzzy body. When the bee visits the next flower, some pollen rubs off. This helps the plant make seeds. Apple and cherry trees need bees or other insects to carry their pollen.

texts.title: Eight Arms and Three Hearts
paras: An octopus is an ocean animal with a soft body and eight arms. Each arm is covered with round suckers. The suckers help the octopus hold on to rocks and grab food, such as crabs. An octopus has no bones at all. It has three hearts, and its blood is blue.
An octopus also has a large brain for its size. It can solve puzzles, such as opening a jar to get the food inside. Scientists say octopuses are very smart.

texts.title: Staying Safe
paras: An octopus lives in the ocean, where many animals want to eat it. To stay safe, an octopus can change the color of its skin in less than a second. It can look like sand, rocks, or seaweed. With no bones in its body, it can squeeze into a tiny hole.
If a fish comes too close, an octopus can squirt a cloud of dark ink. Many octopuses hide in a den in the day and hunt crabs at night. Some pull shells in front of the door with their eight arms.

texts.title: Growing Up in a Pond
paras: Many frogs begin life as tiny eggs in a pond. A mother frog can lay hundreds of eggs at a time, in a jelly that keeps them together. A tadpole hatches from each egg. It has a tail for swimming and gills for breathing underwater.

As the tadpole grows, it sprouts back legs and then front legs. Its tail gets shorter and shorter. It grows lungs and starts to breathe air. The change takes many weeks. Then the young frog hops onto land near the pond and starts to catch and eat insects.

texts.title: Time for Dinner

A frog does not chew its food. It swallows it whole. When a frog swallows, its eyes sink down into its head, and they help push the food down its throat! Then the frog hops to a new spot to wait again.

texts.title: Shining at Night
paras: The Moon does not make its own light. Sunlight shines on the Moon's gray rocks and dust and bounces off, the way light bounces off a wall. The Moon has no air, so there is no wind there, and its sky is always black.

The Moon travels around Earth about once a month. As it moves, we see different amounts of its sunny side. That is why the Moon seems to change shape. These shapes are called phases. A full moon looks like a circle. A crescent moon looks like a thin curve.

texts.title: The First Visitors
paras: In 1969, two astronauts became the first people to walk on the Moon. They flew there with a third astronaut in a spacecraft named Apollo 11, which traveled around Earth and then on to the Moon. The trip took about four days.

The Moon has no air to breathe, so the astronauts wore space suits. They picked up Moon rocks to bring back to Earth. The footprints they left are still there today, because the Moon has no wind or rain to wipe them away. The Moon travels around Earth, and so do the footprints!

paras: Most bats come out at night to find insects to eat. To find their way in the dark, many bats use their ears. A bat makes high squeaks as it flies. The sound bounces off things around it and comes back as an echo.

By listening to the echoes, a bat can tell where a moth is. Then it catches the moth and eats it. This way of finding things is called echolocation. Most of the squeaks are too high for people to hear.

texts.title: Friends in the Night Sky
paras: Bats are mammals, and they are the only mammals that can truly fly. Their wings are made of thin skin stretched over long finger bones. Most bats come out at night and sleep during the day.

Bats help people in many ways. Many bats eat huge numbers of insects, such as mosquitoes and moths. Some bats drink nectar from flowers and carry pollen, the way bees do. Other bats eat fruit and drop the seeds, which helps new trees grow.

texts.title: Flippers and a Shell
paras: Sea turtles spend almost their whole lives swimming in the ocean. Instead of feet, they have flippers that work like paddles. Like all turtles, a sea turtle has a shell. Many land turtles can pull their heads into their shells, but a sea turtle cannot.
Sea turtles breathe air, just like people. A sea turtle must swim up to the top of the water to take a breath. When it is resting, it can hold its breath for a long time, sometimes for hours.

texts.title: Hatching Time
paras: A mother sea turtle crawls out of the ocean onto a sandy beach at night. She digs a hole with her back flippers and lays about one hundred eggs inside. Then she covers them with sand and goes back to the water.

About two months later, the baby turtles hatch, each with a tiny shell. They dig out of the sand and hurry toward the ocean. Birds and crabs eat some of them on the way. The ones that reach the water swim out to sea, coming up now and then to breathe air.

paras: Many spiders spin webs out of silk. The silk comes from body parts called spinnerets at the back of the spider. Some threads of a web are sticky, and some are not. The spider walks on its eight legs along the threads that are not sticky.
When an insect flies into the web, it gets stuck. The web shakes, and the spider feels it. The spider rushes over and wraps the insect in silk to eat later. Some spiders spin a new web every day.
